newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese companies enjoy hot sales amid heatwave.
newsitem.headline: Japanese companies enjoy hot sales amid heatwave.

text.p: An unexpected heatwave appears to have helped Japanese consumers, burdened with a higher consumption tax since April, loosen their tight purse strings.
Economists said the hot weather may push up private spending, which has been dampened by the rise in the national sales tax from three percent to five percent on April 1.

"The hot weather has helped to boost sales of summer apparel and other seasonal goods considerably and it is likely to be a positive factor for consumption," said Fuji Securities chief market economist Yasunari Ueno.
A government official said the heatwave could cheer up the outlook for economic recovery, which some feared could have been derailed by the increased tax.

"We must keep a close watch on the effect of the heatwave. If this creates (demand) for goods, it will brighten corporate business confidence through improvements in their plant utilisation rates and earnings," a government official said.
On the Tokyo Stock Exchange on Tuesday, shares of firms which benefit from a heatwave, rose on growing expectations of a positive impact on their earnings.
Share prices of firms such as Daikin Industries Ltd, a major maker of commercial air conditioners, and Asahi Breweries Ltd, surged on the back of increased sales.
Beer makers, whose sales typically rely on high temperatures, were more than happy.
"We have seen shipments of our beer grow more than 10 percent year-on-year since the beginning of July," said a spokesman for Kirin Brewery Co Ltd.
Kirin, Japan's biggest beer maker, operated two of its domestic breweries last weekend to meet the strong demand.
The company currently plans to operate on at least two more weekends in July, the spokesman said.
According to Kirin's estimates, beer sales grow by 2.4 percent with every one degree Celsius rise in temperatures.

Temperatures in Tokyo reached 37.7 degrees C on Saturday, 11 degrees higher than the average temperature for that day over the past seven years. It was also the hottest day in Tokyo in the month of July since the government's Meteorological Agency begun taking statistics in 1923.
Home appliance makers are also banking their hopes on sales of air conditioners as demand declined sharply after the consumption tax was increased.
A spokesman for Hitachi Ltd said the company is now hard-pressed to keep up with ballooning orders.
"We drew up our production plan based on expectations of a cool summer. We wish we had known earlier," said the spokesman.
A spokeswoman for Printemps, a trendy department store in Tokyo's central Ginza district, said sales of swimsuits on the first weekend of July surged by 40 percent from the same period last year.
"Sales of parasols, sandals and yukata (traditional Japanese summer kimonos), are also doing extremely well," she said.

A spokesman for Snow Brand Milk Products Co Ltd, a top maker of dairy products, said ice cream sales start picking up when temperatures rise above 25 degrees C, but once the mercury rises above 30, demand for Popsicles overtake ice cream.

"It is still too early to tell whether the sweltering heat will continue and we are holding back on Popsicle production. The E-coli bacteria outbreak depressed sales last year and this year we have heard people are afraid of being infected by the bacteria, so we are taking a cautious stance," he said.
